Found one: OdinPlus-Basements — a placeable basement piece, made for Valheim 1.0. It's what you want for digging under your base.

One catch before I add it: it has to be installed on the server **and on every player's own machine**. Each of you will need to install it (and the mod loader) through r2modman or Thunderstore Mod Manager before you can join — I can't do that part for you. tool_calls.name: game_guide
tool_calls.result:
Some of valheim's settings are not stored in any config file on this server — they are read from the environment when the game starts, and the only place an instance can set them is .grizzly/env, at the top of the data directory. It is always there, often empty. Don't go looking for a config file for these: there isn't one, and searching for it is time spent on something that cannot be found.

Exactly these settings do anything in that file, and the rest are ignored: SERVER_PASS, SERVER_NAME, SERVER_PUBLIC and CROSSPLAY. A line naming anything else is dropped when the game launches, so the change will look like it worked and won't have.

Read the file first to see what's already set, then change it like any other config file — one setting at a time — and restart to apply it. That restart self-guards: if the game refuses a value and won't start, the previous version of the file is restored and the server restarted automatically, and you'll be told. So a value you're unsure of is worth trying rather than talking around; afterwards, read_logs to confirm it took rather than assuming.

Here is how mods work on valheim. These rules are specific to this game — another game's identifiers and install steps are different, so ask for its guide separately rather than reusing this one.

Never name a mod from memory. Mods here are identified by a Namespace-Name pair — `ValheimModding-Jotunn`, not `jotunn` and not a display name — and a name that doesn't exist stops the server from starting. Use search_mods with this game to find candidates, then mod_info on the exact pair to get the version to install, what else it needs, and where it has to be installed. A search result deliberately carries no version, so mod_info is a required step and not a double-check.

Where a mod has to be installed is the thing to get right before anything else. The registry reports one of four answers: the server only, which costs the players nothing; the server *and* every player's machine, which means every one of them has to install that file and the mod loader themselves and nothing you do on the server does it for them; players' machines only, which means there is nothing to install server-side at all and you should say so rather than adding it; or not stated, which happens often — libraries in particular are usually untagged — and means you should point them at the mod page rather than guess. When a mod needs installing on players' machines too, say so and ask whether they still want it before you touch anything.

Installing is a config change to a single file: .grizzly/mods, at the top of the server's data directory. It is always there, often empty. One mod per line, written as Namespace-Name-1.2.3 — pinned to exactly the version mod_info reported, because a pinned list reinstalls identically every restart and can be rebuilt from the server's own copy even when the registry is unreachable. Blank lines and lines starting with # are ignored. Read the file first, then change it like any other config file.

Updating every mod is one call, not one per mod: update_mods with mode `check` reports every pinned version that has moved and writes nothing, and mode `apply` rewrites the list. Reach for it for both "are my mods up to date" and "update the mods" — never walk the list with mod_info, which costs a lookup per mod and is where a version gets typed wrong.

List only the mods someone actually asked for. Anything a mod depends on is installed automatically, and the mod loader itself is already part of the image — listing it is refused. To remove a mod, delete its line: the installed set is rebuilt from this file at every start, so a line that isn't there is a mod that isn't installed. That is the opposite of how Minecraft's list works, so don't carry the habit across.

Restart to apply it, and that restart self-guards like any other config change: a line naming a mod that doesn't exist, or a malformed line, stops the server, and the previous version of the file is restored and the server restarted automatically. Afterwards, read_logs shows lines beginning with [mods] naming exactly what was installed, and .grizzly/thunderstore/resolved lists the same thing as plain text — check one of them rather than assuming it worked. Each mod's own settings file appears under the data directory after its first boot and is edited like any other config file; your edits there are never overwritten while the mod is installed, and when you remove a mod its settings file is deleted with it on the next start that comes up cleanly — so a settings file you can still find belongs to a mod that is still installed. Before the first install on a world people have already played on, take a backup_server — putting a world back afterwards is something only an admin can do. Tell them up front that a first install takes a minute or so: every mod is fetched before the world even loads.

A whole modpack moves in one step through an r2modman profile code — a UUID people copy out of r2modman or Thunderstore Mod Manager. This is how modded groups already agree on a pack, so reach for it before going mod by mod. Someone who hands you a code wants import_profile; someone asking how to set their own game up to join wants export_profile, and that one is worth offering unprompted, because the usual reason a modded server "doesn't work" for one player is that their versions have drifted from the server's.

Importing **replaces** the mod list rather than adding to it — read the list first if they meant to add. A code is a *player's* profile, so it lists things the server has no business installing; the import sorts that out and tells you what it left out and why.

That is also why the mod list is the group's whole pack rather than just this server's installs. A line prefixed `client:` — `client:RandyKnapp-EquipmentAndQuickSlots-3.0.2` — names a mod that belongs on the players' machines only: the server installs nothing for it, but it travels with the pack and appears in any code you export. A `client:` line must always carry a version, since nothing works one out for it. Remove either kind by deleting its line.

A code you hand out describes the pack at that moment and cannot be taken back. Say what is in it when you give it out, and mint a fresh one after the mods change rather than pointing anyone at an old one.
